title: A counting characterization of P with NP access
formal:
Does there exist one total counting function \(f\in\#\mathrm P\) such that
\[\mathrm P^f=\mathrm P^{\mathrm{NP}}=\mathrm P^{\mathrm{SAT}}?\]
The oracle for \(f\) returns its exact nonnegative integer value in binary. Both sides are classes of decision problems with deterministic, adaptive polynomial-time oracle access. This asks about the ordinary, unrelativized classes; no auxiliary oracle or complexity separation is assumed.
why: The question asks whether existential search has a precise counting counterpart at the level of computational power. Resolving it would clarify the boundary between deciding existence, counting witnesses and the polynomial hierarchy, while a negative answer would also separate P from NP.
status_note: Source-open: Fortnow’s 18 August 2021 manuscript, §6.5/Conjecture 6.3, explicitly poses the unrelativized equality and the weaker containment question. Theorem 1.1 and §§2–4 of the 2009 Theory of Computing paper were read for the hierarchy comparison. Bounded subsequent-work searches through 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution; this is not an exhaustive current-openness certification. The equivalence of the two simulation requirements and the P=NP observation are elementary editorial consequences of the stated definitions, not new attributed theorems.

progress.text: Toda’s containment \(\mathrm{PH}\subseteq\mathrm P^{\#\mathrm P}\), with a short complete proof published by Fortnow in 2009, explains the strength available from unrestricted complete counting.
Conjecture 6.3 isolates the existence of a potentially weaker counting function with exactly NP-oracle polynomial-time power; the source also records the weaker hierarchy-bounded containment as open.

importance.reason: A structural comparison of two central forms of computation: NP-oracle decision and exact witness counting. Its connection to the polynomial hierarchy and the consequence of a negative answer make it substantial beyond one representation or reduction.

sentences: The target asks for one #P counting function whose polynomial-time oracle power is exactly P with an NP oracle.
The count is an exact nonnegative integer returned in binary, and oracle queries may be adaptive.
The same function must allow SAT decisions while itself being computable using SAT queries.
Complete counting can already capture the whole polynomial hierarchy, so choosing a weaker count is a substantive requirement.
The question concerns ordinary complexity classes, separately from the source’s request for a relativized counterexample.

definitions:
All inputs and oracle queries are finite binary strings. Write \(|x|\) for the full bit length, and let \(\mathbb N\) include zero. A function \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\mathbb N\) belongs to \(\#\mathrm P\) if there are one deterministic polynomial-time predicate \(V(x,y)\) and one polynomially bounded, polynomial-time computable length function \(p:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) such that
\[f(x)=\bigl|\{y\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}:V(x,y)=1\}\bigr|\]
for every string \(x\). Each witness string is counted once. This is an exact count, not a signed difference of counts, an approximation, a parity bit or a mere indication of nonemptiness. In particular, \(f(x)\le2^{p(|x|)}\), so its binary representation has polynomial length; zero is encoded as the one-bit string 0.

Use uniform deterministic multitape oracle Turing machines. A machine has one finite program independent of input length, a read-only input tape and ordinary work, query and answer tapes. It writes a query string \(z\), invokes the fixed oracle and receives the canonical binary expansion of \(f(z)\). The oracle's internal computation is not charged; writing queries, reading answer bits and all subsequent computation are charged. The oracle response is exact. The machine must halt on every input of length \(n\) in at most \(C(n+1)^d\) steps for some fixed positive integers \(C,d\). It may make polynomially many queries, and later queries may depend on earlier answers. There is no advice, randomness, nondeterminism or second oracle. The union over such machines defines the language class \(\mathrm P^f\); different languages may use different programs and polynomial bounds, but all use the same \(f\).

For the decision oracle, fix an explicit binary encoding of Boolean formulas as finite AND/OR/NOT expression trees with variable identifiers. SAT returns 1 exactly for a well-formed satisfiable formula, and returns 0 on an unsatisfiable formula or malformed string. The whole formula is written explicitly, including identifiers and delimiters. Since SAT is NP-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions, \(\mathrm P^{\mathrm{NP}}\) here means \(\mathrm P^{\mathrm{SAT}}\). An SAT-oracle machine receives one exact decision bit per query; it has the same uniformity, adaptive access and polynomial running-time convention. \(\mathrm{FP}^{\mathrm{SAT}}\) denotes the analogous functions computed by machines that output a finite binary string instead of a decision bit.

The displayed equality has the equivalent concrete requirements
\[\mathrm{SAT}\in\mathrm P^f\qquad\text{and}\qquad f\in\mathrm{FP}^{\mathrm{SAT}}.\]
Thus one fixed counting function must be strong enough to decide SAT, yet every value of that function must be computable using only polynomial time and SAT queries. Equality implies the second requirement because querying a particular output bit of \(f\) is a decision problem in \(\mathrm P^f\), and there are polynomially many bits. The converse follows by replacing oracle calls by the stated simulations. This equivalence fixes the decision/function distinction; it adds no single-query, nonadaptive or parsimonious-reduction requirement.

The existential quantifier is over all \(\#\mathrm P\) functions. The selected function need not be \(\#\mathrm P\)-complete or count satisfying assignments of its input formula. There is no requirement that one algorithm uniformly discover a suitable function from an arbitrary verifier. A refutation must rule out every possible fixed \(\#\mathrm P\) function, not just the familiar \(\#\mathrm{SAT}\) function.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence statement. A positive answer must define one total \(f\), prove its \(\#\mathrm P\) representation and prove both class containments, with the uniform polynomial-time oracle simulations justified. Equivalently, prove both concrete requirements in the definitions. A negative answer must prove that every \(f\in\#\mathrm P\) fails at least one containment. An oracle-relative separation, a conditional statement assuming an unproved class separation, an approximate count, or one candidate that fails does not settle this unrelativized question. The target is exact class equality; numerical approximation tolerances do not apply.

source_formulation.text: Conjecture 6.3 asks whether a #P function can have exactly the polynomial-time oracle power of NP.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Conjecture 6.3; the surrounding section also asks a separate oracle-construction question

context_blocks.text: A SAT oracle reports whether a witness exists. A counting oracle can disclose far more information by reporting how many witnesses exist. This question asks whether some genuine count has exactly the power of repeated SAT decisions, with neither a deficit nor a surplus of computational power.

The familiar choice \(\#\mathrm{SAT}\) counts all satisfying assignments. Toda’s theorem gives \(\mathrm{PH}\subseteq\mathrm P^{\#\mathrm{SAT}}\), where \(\mathrm{PH}=\bigcup_{i\ge0}\Sigma_i^{\mathrm P}\), \(\Sigma_0^{\mathrm P}=\mathrm P\), and \(\Sigma_{i+1}^{\mathrm P}=\mathrm{NP}^{\Sigma_i^{\mathrm P}}\). Therefore equality with \(\mathrm P^{\mathrm{NP}}\) for this particular complete counting function would collapse the whole polynomial hierarchy to \(\mathrm P^{\mathrm{NP}}\). This is a conditional consequence, not a proof that this candidate or every other candidate fails.

Fortnow places the question next to the checkability of SAT: whether a randomized polynomial-time checker can assess the answer of a purported SAT solver using that solver as an oracle. The source describes a possible connection between counting and checking, not a proved equivalence between the two open questions.

The 2021 source does not even know a counting function satisfying the weaker pair \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm P^f\subseteq\mathrm{PH}\). That observation is dated context; the benchmark retains the stronger equality of Conjecture 6.3.

The surrounding article studies relativization: what happens when machines receive an additional fixed oracle. Its section heading requests an oracle world with no such counting characterization. That separate construction would not refute the ordinary-world target stated here.

If \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), the constant-zero counting function already meets the equality. Consequently, a negative answer here would imply \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\). This is an immediate consequence of the definitions, not an additional hypothesis in the card.
